paper_a.title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

paper_b.title: Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning

metadata.description: SimCLR and MoCo are competing frameworks for unsupervised visual representation learning by contrastive (InfoNCE-style) losses on two augmented views of an image. They share the same problem, the same loss family, the instance-discrimination pretext task, and a closely related encoder-then-similarity training loop, but differ fundamentally in how negatives are supplied: SimCLR enlarges the in-batch dictionary (very large minibatches with symmetric in-batch negatives, plus an MLP projection head and aggressive augmentations), while MoCo decouples dictionary size from batch size via a FIFO queue of past keys whose encoder is a momentum moving average of the query encoder. Almost every conceptual node in one paper has a counterpart in the other, but several MoCo-specific contributions (queue, momentum encoder, shuffling BN) and SimCLR-specific contributions (NT-Xent symmetric loss, projection head, color-augmentation emphasis, LARS large-batch tricks) have no analogue.

matches.explanation: Both papers state the same overarching problem: learn an image representation from unlabeled data so that downstream tasks (linear evaluation / fine-tuning, ImageNet and transfer benchmarks for SimCLR; detection/segmentation/classification for MoCo) succeed. SimCLR phrases it around linear / semi-supervised / fine-tuned downstream classification, MoCo around fine-tuned downstream vision tasks; the underlying problem is identical.

SimCLR's `Contrastive prediction task' (identify the matching positive view inside a set) plays the same role as MoCo's `Dynamic Dictionary Look-up' problem (match query q to its positive key k+ among many negatives). Both are operationalisations of the instance-discrimination pretext task (DP229.6, cited from Wu et al. 2018 by MoCo and implicit in SimCLR via the augmentation-pair construction). The framing differs: SimCLR thinks of it as a 2N-way in-batch identification, MoCo as a (K+1)-way dictionary look-up against a separately maintained dictionary.

SimCLR's stochastic data augmentation module produces two correlated views t(x), t'(x) treated as a positive pair; MoCo's instance-discrimination pretext task defines positives as two random augmentations / views of the same image. Same construction, different naming: SimCLR packages it as a definition of the augmentation operator; MoCo packages it as a (cited) pretext task definition. Both sit upstream of the encoder and supply the positive pair.

SimCLR splits its encoding pipeline into a base encoder f and a separate MLP projection head g (h then z = g(h)); MoCo has a single query encoder f_q and key encoder f_k (no separately defined projection head in the main definitions). The base encoder f corresponds to f_q for the query side, and the projection head is a SimCLR-specific addition with no MoCo counterpart of its own — bundled here because the encoded representations in MoCo's q = f_q(x_q) play the same downstream role as SimCLR's z = g(f(x)).

SimCLR explicitly defines cosine similarity sim(u,v) = u^T v / (||u|| ||v||). MoCo writes its loss using a generic dot product q . k_+ and only later (in the algorithm pseudocode) implicitly normalises features; cosine similarity is not lifted to a separate definition node. Treated as paper-original SimCLR formalism with no L1 counterpart in MoCo's graph.

SimCLR's NT-Xent per-pair loss and MoCo's InfoNCE loss are the same softmax-cross-entropy contrastive objective: -log( exp(sim(z_i,z_j)/tau) / sum_k exp(sim(z_i,z_k)/tau) ) versus -log( exp(q.k_+/tau) / sum_i exp(q.k_i/tau) ). NT-Xent is SimCLR's name for InfoNCE applied to symmetric in-batch positive pairs with explicit l2 normalisation; the underlying expression matches term-for-term up to notation. MoCo flags InfoNCE as external (CPC, Oord et al. 2018), SimCLR's NT-Xent is paper-original packaging of the same loss.

SimCLR's symmetric minibatch loss L = (1/2N) sum_k [ ell(2k-1,2k) + ell(2k,2k-1) ] symmetrises NT-Xent over both directions of every positive pair within the batch. MoCo's InfoNCE is asymmetric (query-vs-key), so there is no symmetric-minibatch counterpart. Paper-original SimCLR formula with no MoCo analogue.

SimCLR introduces NT-Logistic and Margin Triplet losses purely as comparison baselines for its loss-ablation claim ClP228.7. MoCo only uses the InfoNCE loss and offers no analogous alternative-loss definitions.

Both papers identify a BN-leakage problem when the positive pair shares a device's BN statistics, and both fix it with a BN modification. SimCLR uses Global BN (aggregate BN statistics across all devices) while MoCo uses Shuffling BN (shuffle the sample order between GPUs before encoding the keys, then unshuffle). Same goal — break the per-device BN shortcut that lets the network identify positives via batch statistics — different mechanism. This is one of the cleanest CF (competing frameworks) signals in the alignment.

MoCo's `Dictionary as a Queue' is the central data-structure innovation of MoCo: maintain a FIFO queue of past mini-batch keys, decoupling dictionary size K from the mini-batch size. SimCLR has no such queue; its dictionary is exactly the in-batch 2N-1 negatives. Paper-original MoCo contribution with no SimCLR counterpart.

MoCo's momentum update theta_k <- m theta_k + (1-m) theta_q (and its definition / equation pair) is the second core innovation: the key encoder is an EMA of the query encoder, so dictionary keys remain consistent even as f_q changes. SimCLR encodes both views with a single encoder f trained directly by SGD, so no momentum encoder, no EMA update. Paper-original MoCo contribution.

Both algorithms are the main learning procedure of their paper: minibatch SGD that, per minibatch, applies two augmentations to each example, encodes them, computes pairwise similarities, and minimises an InfoNCE/NT-Xent contrastive loss. They diverge in three substantive ways aligned with the CF hypothesis: (i) MoCo maintains a key-queue and computes the loss against (positive in current batch, K negatives in queue) while SimCLR uses (positive in current batch, 2N-2 in-batch negatives); (ii) MoCo updates f_k via the momentum rule and stops gradient on keys, SimCLR back-props through both views with one shared encoder; (iii) SimCLR adds a discardable projection head g and uses LARS for very large batches. Same recipe template, different negative-sampling mechanism.

Composite L2-vs-L2 alignment of the inner step DAGs (parent L1 algorithm match emitted above per the §Level-2 rule). The two procedures share the augmentation step (ASP228.1 ~ ASP229.3), the encode step (ASP228.2 ~ ASP229.4), the similarity / logits step (ASP228.3 ~ ASP229.5), the InfoNCE-style loss step (ASP228.4 ~ ASP229.6), and an SGD step (ASP228.5 ~ ASP229.7). MoCo additionally has an explicit initialisation step (ASP229.1), an outer mini-batch loop (ASP229.2), a momentum-update step (ASP229.8), and an enqueue/dequeue step (ASP229.9) — the mechanism-defining steps of MoCo with no SimCLR counterpart. SimCLR has a `return encoder, drop projection head' step (ASP228.6) with no MoCo analogue (MoCo has no projection head to drop).

SimCLR's color distortion augmentation is given a separate algorithm node because color augmentation strength is a load-bearing design choice for SimCLR (see ClP228.1, ClP228.2). MoCo uses standard augmentations (random crop, color jitter, grayscale, etc.) but does not break out a color-augmentation algorithm and does not emphasise color augmentation strength as a contribution. Paper-original SimCLR contribution.

SimCLR's claim that composing augmentations (especially crop + color) is critical is a SimCLR-original empirical finding. MoCo does not lift augmentation composition to a claim-level statement; it uses standard augmentations without an explicit composition claim.
SimCLR's claim that contrastive learning needs stronger color augmentation than supervised has no MoCo counterpart; MoCo does not run an analogous augmentation-strength comparison against supervised.

SimCLR's claim that unsupervised contrastive learning benefits more than supervised from larger models is a SimCLR-specific scaling claim. MoCo reports R50w4x results (in ExP229.1) but does not lift the size-scaling observation to a labelled claim node.
SimCLR's nonlinear-projection-head claim (head g improves features and h beats z) is SimCLR-specific. MoCo has no projection head and no corresponding claim.

SimCLR's claim about the importance of l2 normalisation and temperature is a SimCLR-original empirical claim. MoCo also uses temperature tau and normalised features but does not lift them to a claim with a full ablation in the extracted graph.

SimCLR's claim that larger batch sizes help (because they supply more negatives) and MoCo's `large and consistent dictionaries' desideratum address the same underlying observation: more negatives help contrastive learning. SimCLR's response is to scale the batch (with LARS); MoCo's response is to decouple dictionary size from batch size (queue) while preserving consistency (momentum encoder). Same observation, opposite engineering responses — exactly the CF axis of this pair. Cross-type (claim vs remark) match justified by shared empirical content.
SimCLR's claim that NT-Xent outperforms NT-Logistic and Margin losses is supported by SimCLR's own loss ablations; MoCo does not run an analogous loss comparison.

Same downstream evaluation: pretrain unsupervisedly on ImageNet, freeze, train a linear classifier, report ImageNet top-1. SimCLR ResNet-50 (4x): 76.5% top-1 / 93.2% top-5; MoCo ResNet-50: 60.6%, R50w4x: 68.6%. Same protocol, directly comparable numbers — a textbook CF benchmark co-occurrence. SimCLR is substantially higher on this metric, illustrating the trade-off between mechanism (MoCo's queue lets you do this on small GPUs) and headline accuracy (SimCLR pushes harder on batch size + augmentation + projection head).

Both papers test transfer to many downstream tasks: SimCLR fine-tunes ResNet-50 (4x) on 12 image classification datasets; MoCo fine-tunes on PASCAL VOC detection, COCO detection / instance segmentation, COCO keypoint, dense pose, LVIS, Cityscapes, VOC-seg, and iNaturalist classification. The common claim is `unsupervised pretraining transfers competitively / better than supervised'. Mapping is many-to-many: SimCLR's transfer-classification suite is one node; MoCo splits its transfer story into multiple example nodes by task family. Different downstream-task ecosystems but same `transfer benchmark' role.
MoCo's open question about better pretext tasks (e.g. masked auto-encoding analogous to BERT) is paper-specific; SimCLR has no open-problem nodes.

MoCo's open problem of large-mini-batch optimisation for end-to-end contrastive training directly anticipates the engineering challenge that SimCLR addressed (with LARS + sqrt LR scaling, RP228.2/RP228.3) — but as an open question on the MoCo side it has no `node' answer in SimCLR's graph; SimCLR just engineered around it.
